title: State and immutability
summary: useState, why state is a snapshot, batching and updater functions, replacing objects and arrays instead of mutating them, and where state should live.

sections.title: State is a snapshot
sections.body:
`const [count, setCount] = useState(0)` gives you the value **for this render** and a setter. Calling the setter does not change `count` in the current function call; it asks React to render again with the new value. So code after `setCount(count + 1)` still sees the old `count`.

The initial value is used only on the first render. To compute an expensive initial value once, pass a function: `useState(() => parse(raw))`, not `useState(parse(raw))`, which would run `parse` on every render.

sections.title: Batching and updater functions
sections.body:
React **batches** state updates: every setter call in the same event (and, since React 18, in timeouts, promises and native handlers too) produces one re-render. Because each call reads the same snapshot, `setCount(count + 1)` three times adds 1, not 3.

Pass an **updater function** when the next value depends on the previous one: `setCount(c => c + 1)` three times adds 3, because React queues the functions and runs them in order.
sections.code:
setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1) // +1
setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(c => c + 1) // +3

sections.title: Replace, never mutate
sections.body:
React compares state with `Object.is`. If you mutate an object or array and set the same reference, React may skip the render, and memoised children and effects will not see a change. Always create a new value:

- Objects: `setUser({ ...user, name })`; nested: `{ ...user, address: { ...user.address, city } }`.
- Add: `[...items, item]`. Remove: `items.filter(i => i.id !== id)`. Update: `items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: !i.done } : i)`.
- Sort or reverse a copy: `items.toSorted(compare)` or `[...items].sort(compare)`.

Spread is **shallow**: nested objects are still shared, so copy every level you change.

sections.title: Where state lives
sections.body:
Keep state as **minimal** as possible and derive the rest during render: store `items` and `filter`, compute `visibleItems` instead of storing it. Duplicated or derived state drifts out of sync.

When two components need the same state, **lift it up** to their closest common parent and pass it down with callbacks. State is tied to a component's **position in the tree**: the same component at the same position keeps its state; changing its `key` or rendering a different type at that position resets it.

pitfalls: Reading state right after setting it and expecting the new value.
Using `count + 1` three times instead of an updater.
`push`, `splice`, `sort` or assigning a property on state.
Storing values you could compute from props or other state.
Calling a setter unconditionally during render, which loops forever ("Too many re-renders").

gotchas.question: What does the button show after one click?
gotchas.code:
const [n, setN] = useState(0)
<button onClick={() => { setN(n + 5); setN(m => m + 1) }}>{n}</button>
gotchas.answer: 6. The first call queues "replace with 5"; the updater then runs on 5 and gives 6.

gotchas.question: What logs after one click?
gotchas.code:
const [n, setN] = useState(0)
function onClick() { setN(n + 1); setTimeout(() => console.log(n), 1000) }
gotchas.answer: 0. The timeout closes over the `n` of the render in which the click happened.

gotchas.question: Why does this list not update on screen?
gotchas.code: function add() { todos.push({ id: Date.now(), text }); setTodos(todos) }
gotchas.answer: The array was mutated and the same reference was set, so `Object.is` says nothing changed and React bails out. Use `setTodos([...todos, newTodo])`.
